name: Whole-food / unprocessed diet

lead: A whole-food or unprocessed diet avoids ultra-processed products in favour of foods close to their natural form. Appearance-focused communities adopt it for skin, leanness and facial puffiness.
Observational studies link high ultra-processed food intake with obesity and several diseases, but the category is debated and no study has tested appearance outcomes of cutting it.

paras: The NOVA classification groups foods by degree of industrial processing. Proposed links to outcomes include energy density, additives and eating patterns, though reference material says mechanisms are unclear.
No notable harms are documented for eating whole foods; critics of the UPF concept note some processed foods are nutritious and that broad condemnation may be oversimplified.

lead: A whole-food or unprocessed diet emphasises foods in minimally processed form and limits ultra-processed foods (UPFs), a category defined by the NOVA classification proposed by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of São Paulo in 2009 and 2010 [1]. In looksmaxxing communities it is promoted for general health, leanness and skin or face appearance.

Observational meta-analyses link higher UPF consumption with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and mortality, but critics say the concept is poorly defined and the evidence largely observational [1]. No study was found on how cutting UPFs affects facial or skin appearance.
infobox: General health, leanness, skin and face appearance

paras: NOVA sorts foods by processing rather than nutrient content. UPFs are industrial formulations with many ingredients, often containing sugars, oils, salt and additives rarely used in home cooking [1]. Whole-food diets reduce these in favour of minimally processed items.

A 2023 meta-analysis linked each 10 percent increase in UPF intake with about 12 percent higher type 2 diabetes risk, a 2024 meta-analysis found about 17 percent higher cardiovascular risk at the highest versus lowest intake, and a 2025 meta-analysis found about 15 percent higher all-cause mortality [1]. A 2024 BMJ umbrella review noted heterogeneity and unclear mechanisms [1].

Critics argue the term is poorly defined and does not assess nutrient content or amount eaten. In a 2022 debate, Arne Astrup argued NOVA misclassifies foods and relies on observational data, while Monteiro argued associations are consistent and mechanisms plausible; both agreed more research is needed [1]. The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition recommended further research, while several Latin American countries recommend avoiding UPFs [1].

No studies found on appearance outcomes. Reference material notes that clinical trial evidence on UPFs and weight is limited and that an often-cited trial has been criticised for not controlling macronutrient profile [1].

lore.intro: Whole-food eating appears in skin, face-fat and general health threads as a baseline habit.

claims.claim: Cutting ultra-processed food improves skin and reduces facial bloating.

timeline.event: Monteiro and colleagues propose the NOVA framework; formal publication in 2010 [1].
